cIQ9IXSUzuM.summary: Monty Montgomery of Xiph.org gives real-time demonstrations of sampling, quantization, bit depth and dither using real audio equipment, including both digital analysis tools and vintage analog bench gear. It shows that sampled audio is not stair-stepped and corrects common misconceptions about digital audio.
cIQ9IXSUzuM.why: HN calls it the gold-standard debunking of audiophile myths and the stair-step misconception, and recommends it as a primer on digital audio.

cZYNADOHhVY.summary: CGP Grey narrates an animated adaptation of Nick Bostrom's Fable of the Dragon-Tyrant. The story uses a dragon that demands a daily toll of lives as a metaphor for aging and society's acceptance of death.
cZYNADOHhVY.why: HN commenters repeatedly recommend it in longevity and aging threads as a concise, fun case for fighting aging.

c12cYAUTXXs.summary: Rick Reed of WhatsApp explains at Erlang Factory 2014 how the service scaled to billions of messages with a very small engineering team. He covers the FreeBSD and Erlang stack, Mnesia usage, server counts and bottleneck work.
c12cYAUTXXs.why: The go-to talk showing how Erlang let a tiny team run a massive messaging system.

cKPlPJyQrt4.summary: James Powell's nearly two-hour PyData talk builds up Python's data model, decorators, generators and context managers, coding live in Vim. It aims to take intermediate programmers toward real Python expertise.
cKPlPJyQrt4.why: HN calls it one of the best technical talks and the clearest explanation of decorators, generators and context managers.

cCOL7MC4Pl0.summary: Jake Archibald's JSConf.Asia 2018 talk "In the Loop" explains the browser event loop, covering tasks, microtasks, requestAnimationFrame, and how rendering interleaves with JavaScript. It uses visual walkthroughs to show why code runs in surprising orders and why setTimeout fixes are unreliable.
cCOL7MC4Pl0.why: HN treats it as the best primer on the event loop, praising its entertaining, easy-to-grasp visual explanations.

cQP8WApzIQQ.summary: The opening lecture of MIT 6.824 Distributed Systems (Spring 2020), introducing the course and core challenges of distributed systems. It begins a playlist that goes on to cover Raft and other consensus papers in Go.
cQP8WApzIQQ.why: Recommended as the standard free course for learning distributed systems from real papers.

cfyWvJdsDRI.summary: A live mock programmer interview in which Casey Muratori interviews game developer Shawn McGrath using a less confrontational format devised by Chris Hecker. It gets deep into technical details while showing how the candidate actually thinks and works.
cfyWvJdsDRI.why: HN cites it as the example of a better alternative to whiteboard and fizzbuzz-style interviews.

cidchWg74Y4.summary: Stuart Halloway argues that simplicity is objective, with a definition and etymology useful to programmers, rather than a subjective buzzword. He shows how this view informs Clojure's design and how to make programs simpler.
cidchWg74Y4.why: HN commenters recommend it, alongside Rich Hickey's talk, for its precise definition of simple versus easy and its implications for code design.

ceFyF9px20Y.summary: Robert Lustig of UCSF updates his sugar talk, arguing that fructose and processed foods drive obesity and metabolic syndrome through their endocrine effects. It is a roughly 90-minute university lecture.
ceFyF9px20Y.why: Recommended as a follow-up to Lustig's original sugar talk for the metabolic details of fructose.

cKxRvEZd3Mw.summary: The first episode of Google's Machine Learning Recipes series. It introduces machine learning and builds a first supervised-learning classifier in about six lines of Python using scikit-learn.
cKxRvEZd3Mw.why: HN commenters recommend it as an approachable first step into machine learning for programmers, with an apples-vs-oranges classifier.

cbeJIwF1pVY.summary: A professor from Illinois compares the cost of building, fueling and operating a nuclear plant against a natural gas plant, using visual charts. It shows how construction time and interest rates dominate, when the investment pays off and when costs cross over.
cbeJIwF1pVY.why: It is the go-to short primer HN commenters cite to explain why nuclear is expensive upfront but cheap to run once the construction debt is paid.

ciStnd9Y2ak.summary: In this TEDxBerlin talk, environmental activist Michael Shellenberger explains why he changed from opposing nuclear power to advocating it, after looking at the evidence on Chernobyl, Fukushima and air pollution.
ciStnd9Y2ak.why: Frequently linked in nuclear-power threads as an eye-opening pro-nuclear argument from a former anti-nuclear activist.

cUzklzVXJwo.summary: Veritasium tells the history of how imaginary numbers arose from the quest for a general solution to the cubic equation, including the duels and secrecy among Renaissance mathematicians. It argues math had to give up the requirement that it mirror reality.
cUzklzVXJwo.why: HN recommends it as a well-visualized, story-driven history of complex numbers, suitable for beginners; some quibble with its framing of algebra and geometry.

cj02_UeUnGQ.summary: Keith Packard traces the 35-year history of the X Window System at linux.conf.au 2020. He uses X to examine licensing, corporate interests and community dynamics in free software, including Unix workstation vendors and Stallman's influence.
cj02_UeUnGQ.why: HN commenters recommend it as the authoritative, firsthand account of how X came to be and why it isn't GPL.

c8iFtaltX-s.summary: Curt Jaimungal interviews biologist Michael Levin of Tufts about consciousness, bioelectricity, emergence, and cancer research. The conversation challenges reductionist views of life.
c8iFtaltX-s.why: HN recommends it as a fascinating, mind-expanding interview on bioelectricity and non-reductionist biology.

cIcbAMO6sxo.summary: A DEF CON 29 talk by Richard Henderson about encoding the EICAR antivirus test string into QR codes and barcodes and scanning them at real systems. Many systems that do not expect such input misbehave or collapse, including a parking garage system.
cIcbAMO6sxo.why: HN commenters recommend it as an entertaining demonstration of how scanners and antivirus software fail on unexpected input.

cn7kTPbW6QQ.summary: Ian Piumarta's 2007 Stanford EE380 lecture on building a dynamic programming environment from the ground up, from the Viewpoints Research Institute's work. It covers the design of a language and system with a recursive design, parsing through code generation, and the COLA architecture.
cn7kTPbW6QQ.why: HN commenters recommend it as a way to understand what the VPRI group considers core, such as supporting any syntax on one JIT compiler and removing boundaries between application and interpreter.

c2J91UG6Fn8.summary: Technology Connections explains why American cars all had the same standardized sealed-beam headlights until 1957. It covers the regulations behind the design and the effect on night visibility.
c2J91UG6Fn8.why: Recommended as a clear explanation of why old headlights looked as they did, and as a case study in mandating requirements versus solutions.

cdiD-9MMpb0.summary: Lex Fridman's long conversation with Andrej Karpathy on Tesla's self-driving approach, Optimus, neural networks, transformers, AGI and more. It also touches on his OpenAI work and working with Elon Musk.
cdiD-9MMpb0.why: Cited for Karpathy's first-hand explanations of camera-only self-driving, transformers and ML trends.

cefnmjtAolY.summary: Edward Kmett's talk to the NY Haskell User Group on the lens library, building from fmap and function composition up to lenses, folds and traversals. It shows how these composable combinators access and modify parts of data structures.
cefnmjtAolY.why: HN calls it dense but mind-blowing, the go-to way to understand lenses through algebraic derivation.

cfwwHa-7Ux8.summary: A three-minute video from Derek Sivers, based on his book Anything You Want, about remembering that the people you deal with online are real people. It contrasts how we treat people face to face with how we treat them online.
cfwwHa-7Ux8.why: Recommended in threads about online hostility as a short reminder to treat strangers as human beings.

clnozSXyF4k.summary: Stargate Studios' 2009 virtual backlot reel shows before-and-after shots in which green screen and compositing replace locations in ordinary TV dramas and comedies. It shows how much of a seemingly real show is computer generated.
clnozSXyF4k.why: HN points to it as a demo of how routinely mundane TV scenes use green screen set replacement, even on TV budgets.

coFIEH3vXPw.summary: Bryan Cantrill's Velocity NYC 2015 talk argues for running containers directly on bare metal rather than layering them on virtual machines. He covers the history of containers and how SmartOS runs Linux workloads via syscall emulation.
coFIEH3vXPw.why: HN commenters recommend it as an engaging and informative explanation of why containers on VMs waste resources and hurt performance.

csyL9EC0S0c.summary: Tef's EMF 2012 talk on lessons from a career in programming, a candid and humorous look at why programming is so often terrible. Slides and a draft script are available online.
csyL9EC0S0c.why: HN lists it among its favorite programming talks and fantastic technical speeches.

czgOWmtGVGs.summary: Kurzgesagt explains the Holocene or Human Era calendar, which adds 10,000 years to the current year to anchor dates to the start of human civilization. It argues this gives a more sensible frame for human history.
czgOWmtGVGs.why: Linked whenever year numbering or the Holocene calendar comes up as the accessible introduction to the idea.

c1UBJbfR-H0.summary: Bobby Powers presents Mesh, a drop-in malloc replacement that eliminates memory fragmentation in unmodified C/C++ programs by compacting memory. The talk covers how it works despite C's fixed object addresses, and its benefits for programs like Redis.
c1UBJbfR-H0.why: Recommended as a great talk on solving fragmentation for C/C++ and runtimes like Ruby and Python without code changes.

c2lgEyNaop4.summary: Frederick Raynal gives a GDC postmortem of Alone in the Dark, the game that helped create the survival horror genre. He covers how the team built it and shows some of the old tools used.
c2lgEyNaop4.why: HN commenters recommend it as a firsthand account from the creator, including the old tooling.

cQO2XTP7QDw.summary: Stuff Made Here builds a handwriting robot and sends its output to a handwriting expert to see whether it can pass as forgery. It walks through the engineering trials and errors along the way.
cQO2XTP7QDw.why: HN commenters recommend it as the physical-machine take on replicating handwriting, with plenty of explained iteration.

cQq2pKNDgIs.summary: A 146-minute Merged Podcast episode in which UAP researcher Ryan Graves talks with economist Robin Hanson about UFOs. Topics include the Great Filter, Hanson's grabby aliens model, and the push for more inquiry into UAPs.
cQq2pKNDgIs.why: HN commenters point to it for Hanson's grabby aliens reasoning as an unusual framework for thinking about UFO behavior and intelligent life in the cosmos.

cTsEzmFamZ8.summary: Joe Rogan's long interview with Andrew Yang during his 2020 presidential run. They discuss universal basic income, automation and his policy proposals.
cTsEzmFamZ8.why: Suggested as a starting point for understanding Yang's capitalist case for UBI, though some note it is long and dated.

cbSu2PXOTOc.summary: A BBC Earth clip from Inside the Animal Mind in which a crow named 007 solves an eight-step puzzle to get a reward. It showcases crow problem-solving.
cbSu2PXOTOc.why: Shared in crow-intelligence threads as a striking demonstration that changes how people see crows.

cjuGCJJUGsg.summary: A short Last Week Tonight segment where John Oliver stages a statistically representative climate debate, with Bill Nye facing a crowd of dissenters. It satirizes false balance in media coverage.
cjuGCJJUGsg.why: Cited to illustrate false balance and the trouble with giving all sides equal weight.

ckSoDW2-wrc.summary: A SciShow episode in which Hank Green introduces five of the most dangerous chemicals, from lethal toxins to substances that explode on contact. It is an entertaining overview of extreme chemical hazards.
ckSoDW2-wrc.why: Recommended as a fun companion to threads about hazardous chemistry, such as hydrofluoric acid and reactive substances.

c52QhiXsmyI.summary: Stuart Halloway introduces REBL, a graphical, interactive tool for browsing Clojure data, extracted from Datomic tools. The talk is from Clojure/conj 2018.
c52QhiXsmyI.why: Recommended as a must-watch Conj talk and as the intro for people who haven't seen REBL, often compared to Jupyter-style tooling.

cBDJDZAo41c.summary: Rick Beato analyzes the music and production of Max Martin through Ariana Grande's Into You, breaking down its layering and songwriting craft.
cBDJDZAo41c.why: HN points to it as an explanation of how Max Martin builds hit songs.

cQWlnTyOSig.summary: PolyMatter examines how universities, especially in the West, depend on foreign and Chinese student tuition and how rankings and incentives distort institutions around that money.
cQWlnTyOSig.why: HN commenters recommend it in college-ranking and higher-ed threads as an explanation of why rankings are a hustle for foreign student revenue.

cVaTc15plVs.summary: First episode of the Norwegian documentary series Hjernevask, in which Harald Eia interviews researchers on the nature versus nurture debate. It focuses on the gender equality paradox and gender differences in career choice.
cVaTc15plVs.why: HN commenters cite it, especially during the Google memo debate, as expert testimony on biological contributions to gender differences.

c0O6UXrOZJo.summary: David Kriesel's FrOSCon talk on how Xerox scancopiers, due to JBIG2 compression, silently replaced digits in scanned documents. He walks through how he discovered the bug and why it is so dangerous.
c0O6UXrOZJo.why: The standard reference whenever HN discusses the Xerox scanner bug or AI and compression that fabricates content.

c1QmB5bW_WQ.summary: A lecture for high school seniors and college freshmen making the case for nuclear power and answering common objections. It is an overview of the channel's more detailed videos on each topic.
c1QmB5bW_WQ.why: Pointed to as a lay-audience explanation of nuclear waste, safety and economics.

cDA3_5982h8.summary: A family video in which kids write instructions for making a peanut butter and jelly sandwich and a parent follows them exactly as written, with comic results. It demonstrates how precise instructions must be.
cDA3_5982h8.why: HN uses it to teach kids computational thinking and as a joke whenever specs, requirements, or LLM prompts are taken too literally.

cIQ36Kt7UVg.summary: Tim Dodd of Everyday Astronaut talks with Elon Musk right after Musk's 2019 Starship presentation. Musk discusses Starship's design, why SpaceX favors conventional engines over aerospikes, and how deleting parts and processes speeds up development.
cIQ36Kt7UVg.why: HN commenters cite it as evidence of Musk's engineering thinking, on questioning requirements, organizational errors mirroring product errors, and Conway's Law, and to argue about whether he is a strong engineer.

cNICGEwmXLU.summary: Joe Armstrong's Strange Loop 2013 talk on building large scalable systems from small isolated parallel components. It covers detecting and correcting errors at run time, changing code while it runs, and how Erlang embodies these principles.
cNICGEwmXLU.why: Pointed to as the canonical pitch for Erlang's fault-tolerance and self-healing model.

cQl6jUjFjp4.summary: Luis von Ahn, creator of CAPTCHA and reCAPTCHA, presents Duolingo at TEDxCMU 2011. The idea is to have millions of people translate the web for free while learning a language, an example of human computation.
cQl6jUjFjp4.why: HN people recommend it as a look at how to get people to eagerly do useful collective work, and as the origin of Duolingo.

cQoQE_HDG8g.summary: A linux.conf.au 2013 talk by a Wayland developer who previously worked on X, telling the history of X and why Wayland was created. It covers X's hardware abstraction and architecture and why they became problematic for modern graphics.
cQoQE_HDG8g.why: Whenever Wayland versus X comes up, HN points to this talk as the authoritative explanation from an X maintainer of why X was replaced.

cYsVvV1aVss.summary: Jessie Frazelle's DockerCon SF 2015 talk on running Docker containers for desktop applications, with fun container hacks and images. It shows how far containers can be pushed beyond servers.
cYsVvV1aVss.why: HN points to it as an illuminating look at what containers really are and as a video companion to running desktop apps in Docker.

coGpmA4saEk.summary: Kirby Ferguson's film argues that creativity is built from copying, transforming and combining existing works, examining music, film and technology. It makes the case that everything is a remix.
coGpmA4saEk.why: HN brings it up in discussions of originality, invention, copying and attribution, including AI art.

ctS8FzqcRug.summary: Swift compiler engineers explain how Swift implements generics using dictionary-passing with reified type metadata. They compare it with Java-style uniform representation and C++ or Rust monomorphization.
ctS8FzqcRug.why: Recommended as the clearest explanation of how Swift generics compile and how that differs from other languages.

cxrkC-pMH_s.summary: Asianometry examines how East Germany tried and failed to build a native semiconductor industry despite heavy investment, including the espionage involved in acquiring Western microelectronics technology.
cxrkC-pMH_s.why: HN commenters share it in chip fab and industrial espionage threads as a well-researched account of East Germany's failed microelectronics effort.

cK8i6aMG9VM.summary: A Jimquisition episode by Jim Sterling demonstrating the Copyright Deadlock, where a video includes footage owned by several companies so that competing YouTube Content ID claims cancel each other out. It highlights how absurd the system is.
cK8i6aMG9VM.why: HN cites it as the clearest explanation of how broken Content ID is and of the deadlock trick for defeating forced monetization.

c-FGwDDc-s8.summary: Part one of a two-part skeptical series examining Elon Musk's past business dealings to test whether he is a self-made genius billionaire.
c-FGwDDc-s8.why: HN mentions it mostly as critical commentary on Musk, with one commenter saying it tempered their view.

c01BlUDIlK4.summary: A clip from Lex Fridman's podcast in which chip architect Jim Keller argues that Moore's Law is not dead and that transistor scaling still has lots of room. He also discusses how to break down hard problems.
c01BlUDIlK4.why: Used to support the argument that chip engineers see plenty of scaling headroom left.

c33AZBnRHks.summary: Matt Parker follows the community effort to speed up his slow Wordle-solving code, which ended up running hundreds of millions of times faster. He walks through the techniques contributors used.
c33AZBnRHks.why: Cited as a fun example of how algorithmic changes can yield enormous performance gains.

c5QF2HjHLSE.summary: Rich Hickey's Clojure Conj 2023 talk on design in practice, covering problem statements, decision matrices, choosing precise words and making decisions in a team.
c5QF2HjHLSE.why: HN draws on it for practical decision-making and problem-framing techniques that apply well beyond Clojure.

c6SUOeAqOjU.summary: Ted Nelson, in his Computers for Cynics series, gives a critical history of Xerox PARC's vision of personal computing. He lists what he sees as the limitations and wrong turns in PARC's approach to the desktop and documents.
c6SUOeAqOjU.why: HN readers treat it as a contrarian counterpoint to the usual PARC mythology, though one commenter noted a few apparent mistakes in it.

cCeeTfsm8bk.summary: MORE is Mark Osborne's Oscar-nominated stop-motion short about a joyless inventor in a drab, conformist society who yearns for his younger days. It won Best Short Film at Sundance in 1999.
cCeeTfsm8bk.why: Brought up in threads about isolation, dystopia and busyness as a moving, relevant short film.

cGqEBvlmFAQ.summary: Matt Gray and Tom Scott review how viewers worked out where they watched the 2017 solar eclipse from, based on clues in their video. They go through the methods people used and how accurate the guesses were.
cGqEBvlmFAQ.why: Used as an example of how effectively internet sleuths can geolocate someone from small details, in privacy and open-source-intelligence discussions.

cHIo96yBf70.summary: A short clip from Person of Interest season 2 where Root and John gain full access to The Machine and its resources. It shows the AI guiding people with targeting data.
cHIo96yBf70.why: Referenced as a fictional illustration of AI-assisted tools and non-visual interfaces.

cNZPRsrwumQ.summary: Boston Dynamics' 2010 demo of BigDog, a quadruped robot that climbs through woods, recovers from kicks, slips on ice and jogs at 5 mph. It was an early showcase of dynamic legged locomotion.
cNZPRsrwumQ.why: Used as the go-to demo of robot resilience when Boston Dynamics comes up.

cNjA0aee07k.summary: BigClive tears down a heated electric shower head of the type common in some countries, often called a suicide shower. He examines the construction and the dangerous fault conditions, such as poor insulation and missing earthing.
cNjA0aee07k.why: HN commenters cite it as a teardown from a YouTuber who dissects appliances, showing live wires in contact with water.

cO1a1Ek-HD0.summary: A clip from Channel 4's Inside Nature's Giants in which Richard Dawkins shows the recurrent laryngeal nerve of the giraffe during a dissection. The nerve takes a long detour down the neck and back up.
cO1a1Ek-HD0.why: HN uses it as the canonical example that evolution is not optimal and can get stuck in local maxima.

cO6txCZpbsQ.summary: Not Just Bikes explains why living in a dense, bikeable Dutch city sharply reduced his family's environmental footprint and improved quality of life. It is a collaboration that continues on Climate Town.
cO6txCZpbsQ.why: HN cites it in threads on sprawl, density, and climate, especially for the point that everything is a short bike ride from downtown Amsterdam.

cOubCHLXT6A.summary: Balaji Srinivasan's Startup School 2013 talk on Silicon Valley's Ultimate Exit, arguing for building alternatives outside existing institutions. It is the primary source for a much-retold and much-distorted idea.
cOubCHLXT6A.why: HN commenters link it as the original talk so people can judge it directly instead of through press retellings.

cPNkH-7PRTk.summary: Rich Hickey presents an extensive introduction to Clojure at the Boston Lisp meeting, assuming prior Lisp knowledge. It covers the language's design decisions relative to other Lisps.
cPNkH-7PRTk.why: Referenced for Hickey's reasoning on design choices such as macros and not building on SBCL.

cZ7LzE3u7Bw.summary: Richard Wilkinson presents data showing that societies with larger income gaps do worse on health, lifespan, trust and other measures. He argues the effects track inequality itself rather than average income. It is a 17-minute TED talk.
cZ7LzE3u7Bw.why: HN commenters cite it in inequality debates as a compact summary of studies linking inequality to worse social outcomes.

ccRtIdlTqlU.summary: James Gosling gives a personal talk at the 50th anniversary seminar of Simula about using the language from 1974 and how it shaped his thinking. He explains how Simula's object model and coroutines influenced the design of Java.
ccRtIdlTqlU.why: HN cites it as a first-hand source that Java's object model traces to Simula 67 rather than Smalltalk.

ceCOhdgRBoc.summary: The first part of an Al Jazeera undercover investigation into the Israel lobby in Britain, covering efforts to influence youth groups and the National Union of Students, including a smear campaign against its president.
ceCOhdgRBoc.why: HN commenters mostly cite it as an investigative documentary on lobbying and influence operations in UK politics, with some presenting it as a critical exposure of the lobby's tactics.

cfSIC8jwbQs.summary: Tom Scott visits Yale's archives to look at a 367-year-old bond from a Dutch water authority that is still paying interest. Finance professor Geert Rouwenhorst explains how it works.
cfSIC8jwbQs.why: Shared as a short, interesting explainer on very long-lived financial instruments.

ciGQCP6HgqI.summary: Jonathan Blow gives a formal, hour-long demo of his Jai compiler focused on the implicit context feature. The context carries things like allocators through a program without explicit parameter passing, and the talk walks through the code.
ciGQCP6HgqI.why: Cited in discussions of memory arenas and allocators as the origin of the implicit context idea that later appeared in Odin and other languages.

cjriSNgFHsM.summary: A vintage demo video of the BeOS operating system running on mid-90s hardware. It shows media playback and window manipulation staying smooth at the same time.
cjriSNgFHsM.why: HN commenters use it to show how responsive BeOS was on very modest hardware compared with Windows and Mac of the era.

ckBfbvOXDvU.summary: Excerpts from W. Edwards Deming's Red Bead Experiment, where workers draw beads from a bowl and are judged on red ones that are largely down to chance. It shows how system variation, not individual effort, drives results.
ckBfbvOXDvU.why: HN cites it as a classic illustration of dysfunctional management, gamed targets, and blaming workers for systemic outcomes.

cqggW08BWO0.summary: A short satirical Onion News Network segment presenting Facebook as a CIA project. It plays on surveillance and data-collection fears.
cqggW08BWO0.why: HN commenters post it whenever surveillance or social-media privacy stories seem to confirm the joke, noting how prescient it looks.

cvZjhWE-3zM.summary: Scott Manley explains the nuclear salt water rocket, Robert Zubrin's concept of a rocket fueled by a rapid nuclear reaction in uranium salt dissolved in water. He covers its extraordinary performance and the dangers of managing it.
cvZjhWE-3zM.why: HN points to it as the go-to accessible video whenever nuclear rocket engines come up.

cwN983PnJoA.summary: Ben Krasnow of Applied Science uses a scanning electron microscope to compare new and worn toothbrush bristles. He shows how the microscopic texturing wears down with use.
cwN983PnJoA.why: HN commenters link it for electron micrographs of fresh versus worn bristles when toothbrush wear comes up.

cHSCmQnGH9Q.summary: CityNerd explains why traffic congestion grows nonlinearly as more cars use a road network, and why adding road capacity tends not to fix it. It covers the consequences for drivers, bus riders, cyclists and pedestrians, and discusses alternatives such as true bus rapid transit.
cHSCmQnGH9Q.why: HN commenters cite it when arguing that congestion is an exponential, feedback-driven problem so widening roads or removing a few cars behaves counterintuitively.

cIQ0yIZgQeE.summary: A 3D-animated walkthrough of a heavy-haul diesel-electric freight locomotive, covering the frame, coupling, draft gear, engine and drive systems. Made in Blender by Animagraffs.
cIQ0yIZgQeE.why: Cited in threads about physical controls and how diesel-electric locomotives actually work.

cISYzA36-ZY.summary: The business card scene from the film American Psycho, in which characters compare their business cards.
cISYzA36-ZY.why: HN invokes it as a joke reference in threads about fonts, typefaces and one-upmanship.

cKUaqFzZLxU.summary: A short George Carlin routine in which he says the owners of the country run a big club and ordinary people are not in it.
cKUaqFzZLxU.why: Quoted whenever commenters want to express that wealth and power are rigged against ordinary people, as in Robinhood or big-tech threads.

cQ54GDm1eL0.summary: A BuzzFeed PSA from 2018 in which a deepfaked Barack Obama, voiced by Jordan Peele, warns about fake video before revealing the trick. It is a one-minute demonstration of AI face and voice manipulation.
cQ54GDm1eL0.why: Used as an early, widely seen example of deepfakes in discussions of fake video and its risks.

cTBx-hHf4BE.summary: The Original Caste's recording of One Tin Soldier synced to Cher's animated video. It is a protest song about war and greed.
cTBx-hHf4BE.why: Posted as a joke or sardonic reply in threads, not as a recommendation.

cTLCfl01zuE.summary: Map Men's Jay Foreman tells the story of how the London Tube map nearly looked very different, including Harry Beck's design and TfL's initial rejection of it. A short, witty history of a design icon.
cTLCfl01zuE.why: Linked in threads on the Tube map and transit map design history.

cXhZvyGtMrk.summary: Footage of Richard Box's art installation in which fluorescent tubes light up in the ground under high voltage power lines, showing the electric fields they produce.
cXhZvyGtMrk.why: HN cites it as a striking demonstration that fluorescent tubes glow under power lines without wiring.

cY_o4A1wzsg.summary: Veritasium answers criticism that his videos make people look stupid, explaining that teaching must address learners' misconceptions and that holding common beliefs inconsistent with science is not stupidity.
cY_o4A1wzsg.why: HN references it in discussions of how misconceptions are studied and how interview editing can make people look foolish.

caVEiitI2vg.summary: h3h3Productions describes how a hacker took over their phone number by getting a SIM card from T-Mobile, and gives security advice such as using a hardware key and an authenticator app.
caVEiitI2vg.why: HN cites it as a well-known example of SIM-swap social engineering that defeated even a carrier PIN, in discussions of SMS-based two-factor authentication.

cbGfc-JBxlY.summary: Gamers Nexus criticizes ASUS over its handling of exploding Ryzen CPUs, overvolting BIOS settings and warranty and support behavior. It re-benchmarks the chips at defaults and argues ASUS eroded customer trust.
cbGfc-JBxlY.why: HN links it as the reference for ASUS's poor treatment of customers, usually with an obligatory tone in ASUS threads.

cc5vN2XReWs.summary: A seconds-long Simpsons clip in which McGill University is called the Harvard of Canada.
cc5vN2XReWs.why: HN uses it as a throwaway reference in threads about college rankings and meaningless 'X of Y' comparisons.

ccyu44rsaZo.summary: A 1967 CBC clip in which Hunter S. Thompson faces a member of the Hell's Angels on television. The studio audience's reactions are a striking window into the era.
ccyu44rsaZo.why: HN commenters cite it as evidence of how much social norms have shifted, given the audience's approval of jokes about domestic violence.

cdgQpa1pUUE.summary: Google's 2012 video of Steve Mahan, who is legally blind, taking a drive in its self-driving car including a drive-through stop. It was shared as a human-interest demonstration of the technology's promise.
cdgQpa1pUUE.why: Cited as an early milestone of autonomous driving, and later as an example of over-optimistic timelines.

cesSRfXqS1Q.summary: A 2-minute clip of US Representative Hank Johnson telling a congressional hearing he feared Guam would become so overpopulated that it would tip over and capsize. Johnson later said he was joking.
cesSRfXqS1Q.why: HN uses it purely as a joke about politicians' grasp of geography and science.

cgm3_jzcNm4.summary: An NBC Today Show correspondent appears to row a canoe in deep storm floodwater, though the water is only about six inches deep. The uploader notes it is a misleading depiction rather than intentional fake news.
cgm3_jzcNm4.why: HN commenters use it as a favorite example of how TV imagery can craft a misleading reality.

chPanW0QWhA.summary: A short Boston Dynamics clip of the DARPA-funded Cheetah quadruped robot hitting 28.3 mph on a treadmill, slightly faster than Usain Bolt's fastest 20 meter split.
chPanW0QWhA.why: Cited as the reference example of a real fast legged robot, often to distinguish it from MIT's Cheetah.

co_DNpTMKXk.summary: A short That Mitchell and Webb Look sketch about the perils of working at home, with an adult-humor punchline. It is British TV comedy.
co_DNpTMKXk.why: Posted as a joke in nearly every thread about working from home.

cpraXaw7dyc.summary: Tesla's short promotional video of Optimus Gen 2, its humanoid robot, with new actuators and sensors, faster hands, faster walking and lower weight.
cpraXaw7dyc.why: Cited only as an example of humanoid robots in development, not as something to learn from.

cwAfJywzk8o.summary: Bryan Cantrill of Joyent describes the experience of porting KVM to SmartOS, an Illumos-based OS, at KVM Forum 2011. He covers the process, the pain points and how DTrace helped.
cwAfJywzk8o.why: Cited as evidence that the KVM port was hard work and as background on Cantrill's illumos virtualization experience.

cyN-CRNrb3E.summary: A TU Wien control-systems demo in which a triple pendulum on a cart is swung up and stabilized using constrained feedforward plus optimal feedback control. It accompanies a 2013 Automatica paper.
cyN-CRNrb3E.why: HN commenters cite it as an example of a hard, chaotic control problem that fast feedback and good control design can solve.
